summary: Light on the island at the mouth of Saint John Harbour, first lit in 1791, beside a quarantine station that held about 2,000 Irish immigrants in 1847. The present tower dates from 1960.

lens.note: Third-order lens and 10-foot lantern placed on the tower in 1915 (LighthouseFriends); the Marine report in the volume printed 1917 lists the third-order dioptric lens among the year's work

structures.type: concrete octagonal, standard Department of Transport plan
structures.note: Fifth light tower at this location (register)

access.note: Canadian Coast Guard property; grounds and tower closed; the breakwater to the island is fenced at its end (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Light begins operating with Samuel Duffy as first keeper (LighthouseFriends)
Lighthouse destroyed by fire in January 1832
Octagonal tower built to replace the one destroyed by fire
Eight sides painted alternately red and white
New keeper's house built
Gas lighting apparatus made on the island put into operation in August 1853; given up some years later
Steam whistle fog signal placed in operation the spring after its November 1859 test
Saxby Gale: landing stage and steps swept away, bell tower blown over, buildings damaged; repairs $438
Lamps and reflectors replaced with a dioptric lens in a new lantern
Storm took the top hamper from the bell boat off the island's east side
Illuminant changed from coal oil to a three-mantle incandescent petroleum vapour light; reported in the Marine report printed 1905 (the report gives no month)
Diaphone fog alarm, air compressed by steam; engine house erected the year before
Storm in which the steamer Lansdowne went to Saint John to recover the bell boat and then tried to recover gas buoys set adrift; the excerpt gives no exact date
Tower raised nine feet by a concrete foundation
Third-order lens and ten-foot Canadian lantern placed on the tower
Quarantine station use ended
Fog alarm building and equipment lost to fire; new installation built
Island buildings demolished (register)
Wooden octagonal tower, reportedly built 1880, torn down
Present concrete octagonal tower built, the fifth light tower at this location
Light de-staffed
Island buildings demolished (register: 1998-1999)
Foghorn silenced despite public outcry

notes_for_editor: Fact-check 2026-10-27. Changes made: (a) LighthouseFriends is copyrighted, so the story now keeps one of its quotations ('the only structure remaining on the island') and paraphrases the rest, including the Saxby Gale sentence, the Duffy, Reed, gas-light and bell-boat sentences, and the 'public outcry' phrase; (b) 'a buoy' corrected to 'bell boat' (LighthouseFriends); (c) 'LighthouseFriends quotes it as producing a most brilliant light' removed: LighthouseFriends does not quote a source there, and the gas paragraph now follows its account of the cost and the abandonment; (d) the new dwelling is cited to the Marine report printed 1908 (scan page 38, printed page 31), not the 1906-07 report; (e) the three-mantle illuminant change is in the Marine report printed 1905 (scan page 72, printed page 59), so the story no longer dates it to 1904 and the event year is 1905; (f) the story said all buildings were demolished in 1955 and 1998-99 and also described remnants, which the register's own entry contradicts; both are now attributed to the register; (g) 'more than forty years between them' is replaced by the list's dates and LighthouseFriends' conflicting text; (h) removed unsupported claims: the 1917 Marine table line (an OCR column table, so the Partridge attribution could not be checked on the image), the 1908 keepers' list line for Hugh Andrews (OCR column table, not checked on the image), the 1904 table row for D. L. Richards (not used; his name in the story comes from LighthouseFriends' list), and 'where the Bay of Fundy meets the city' (no source); (i) footnotes renumbered: the 1917 volume is dropped, the 1919 and 1920 volumes are now 12 and 13, and the 1908 volume (dwelling) is 14. Marine page checks against the corpus page index: 1909 (scan 63, printed 54), 1905 (scan 72, printed 59), 1906 (scan 38, printed 33), 1906-07 (scan 45, printed 38), 1904 (scan 82, printed 69), 1910 (scan 26, printed 19), 1912 (scan 58, printed 51), 1919 (scan 94, printed 95; fiscal year 1917-18), 1920 (scan 97, printed 90; fiscal year 1918-19), 1908 (scan 38, printed 31). Still open: (1) LighthouseFriends is internally inconsistent: its text makes Samuel Duffy the first keeper in 1791 but its list starts him in 1798; it spells the successor Huestis in the text and Huetis in the list; its text says Alexander Reed gave up after nearly forty years, but its list gives 1843 to 1873. The roster uses the list and notes the differences. (2) Quarantine start: LighthouseFriends says set apart in 1785 and used from 1830; the register says established in 1830. Both are in the story. (3) Tower date: the register says 1960; LighthouseFriends says the 1959 demolition preceded the present tower; the record's 1961 comes from the Lighthouse Directory, which was not checked. The story says 1960 with the register cited. (4) The 1909 storm in the Marine report has no date in the excerpt, so the story gives no year. (5) Parks Canada's national historic site page returned navigation text only, so the designation year is not verified here. (6) The Coast Guard List of Lights was not checked for the current characteristic; the record's Fl W 7.5 and its 'sources differ' note stand unverified. (7) Keepers after 1960 are not named in the story. (8) The 1832 fire, 1833 tower, 1840 stripes, 1841 house, 1853 gas plant, 1859 whistle, Foulis priority dispute and 1869 gale rest on LighthouseFriends; the primary House of Assembly and Sessional Paper volumes are not in the local corpus. (9) Access: the island is closed and the story does not describe a route. (10) No photos supplied. (11) D. L. Richards and Hugh Andrews are named from LighthouseFriends' list. The Marine keepers' tables that might corroborate them (1904 and 1908 volumes) are OCR column tables and need an image check before they are cited.
